title: Grading and Road Construction
body: A neglected high spot or a badly banked switchback doesn't just slow the haul cycle — it cracks tires, shifts payload, and turns into one of the ramp incidents that eat a shift. At ADW right now, grading alone isn't even fixing the worst sections; the base material is too hard to hold a profile, which is a different problem than routine grading covers.
keyPoints: Full brake test on the ramp before any grader enters the works — no exceptions, same as any mobile unit.

Grade in the direction of traffic flow unless the Production Foreman calls it otherwise after a risk assessment, and keep the blade retracted and ripper up while traveling to protect the machine's profile.
The 10 m no-go zone parallel to a high wall beats the grading routine every time — no unsupervised grading inside it.
Switchbacks need more than a pass or two: super-elevation, inside-radius clearance, and outside bund integrity all matter because that's where trucks lose visibility and traction.

If a section is failing because the base material won't compact (not just a surface profile issue), grading alone won't fix it — that's the soft-material resurfacing situation flagged in the July 11 shift meeting, not a routine grader job.
apply: If a daily inspection flags a high spot or a rough switchback, check whether it's a profile problem (grade it) or a base-material problem (it needs soft material mixed in) before assigning the grader — treating the second as the first just burns hours without fixing anything.
